messages.body_plain:
Joaquin

Welcome to the list.  There is an abundance of information online that can assist in your organising of your survey.  The most important element is for you to conduct a pilot survey; a small survey to give an idea of the number of bird detections you are likely to encounter per unit of effort (are you intending to walk transects, or conduct the survey using point transects?).  With results of the pilot survey and an idea of the precision you wish to achieve with your survey (coefficient of variation), you can apply some simple formulas to arrive an an approximation for the number of points or length of lines you would need to achieve the desired precision.  Note, this has little to do with the actual size of the study area.

To begin, I suggest you have a look at our online workshop materials:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/ <https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/>
In particular, Chapter 4 has lectures dealing with survey design, and specifically determination of adequate sample size:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/#determination-of-adequate-sample-size
In addition, I would recommend reading of Buckland (2006):

Buckland, S. T. 2006. Point transect surveys for songbirds: robust methodologies. The Auk 123 (2): 345–345.  https://doi.org/10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123[345:psfsrm]2.0.co;2 <https://doi.org/10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123%5B345:psfsrm%5D2.0.co;2>.

After looking at these materials, let us know if you have further questions.

messages.subject: Assessing DSM uncertainty when density is the response variable
messages.subject_clean: Assessing DSM uncertainty when density is the response variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I have created a DSM informed by transect distance sampling data from two visits to each transect. I am now trying to estimate the variance of my DSM with density as my response variable, as per the online practical (i.e. https://workshops.distancesampling.org/stand-intermed-2017/practicals/bookdown/estimating-precision-of-predictions-from-density-surface-models.html).

I first tried using dsm.var.prop but I received the following error message:
> Error in dsm.var.prop(dsm_qp_select, predgrid_var, off.set = predgrid_var$Area): Variance propagation can only be used with count as the response.

I was however able to run dsm.var.gam on my DSM with density as the response variable (output below - as expected my GAM is not very precise...yet). Ultimately I want to report densities per grid cell based on my prediction grid.

So my questions are:
1.Is using dsm.var.gam an appropriate method for assessing a DSM with density as the response variable, or is it more advantageous / informative  to use a different method (e.g. make DSM and prediction grid with count data and use dsm.var.prop in order to interrogate quantiles of differences)?
2. If it is considered worthwhile making a new DSM and prediction grid with count data in order to assess the DSM using dsm.var.prop, would the results of this assessment still be directly applicable/valid for the DSM generated with density as the response, given both are generated using the same data?
3. Also, would you advise / strongly recommend performing some type of cross validation when generating and reporting results of DSMs? If so, is there a particular method you would recommend?

Apologies for my lack of understanding but any help is very much appreciated.

Summary of uncertainty in a density surface model calculated
 analytically for GAM, with delta method

Approximate asymptotic confidence interval:
     2.5%      Mean     97.5%
 145.4002  512.3596 1805.4463
(Using log-Normal approximation)

Point estimate                 : 512.3596
CV of detection function       : 0.03998258
CV from GAM                    : 0.7139
Total standard error           : 366.3673
Total coefficient of variation : 0.7151

As per the online practical, this is my code I tried to use to estimate variance using dsm.var.prop:
> predgrid_var <- predgrid_plot[!is.na <http://is.na>(predgrid_plot$Nhat_qp_select),]
> var_dsm_qp_select <- dsm.var.prop(dsm_qp_select, predgrid_var,
                             off.set=predgrid_var$Area)

DSM model with density as the response variable:
> dsm_qp_select <- dsm(density~ s(x,y, k=18)
                        + s(CHM_mean, k=20)
                        + s(DEM_mean, k=20)
                        + s(NDVI_ALL_mean, k=20)
                        + s(StrAv0to5, k=20)
                        + s(StrAv5to10, k=20)
                        + s(StrAv20to25, k=20),
                        ddf.obj = unifcos.gliders,
                        segment.data = sub_segs,
                        observation.data = obs,
                        family = quasipoisson())

Cheers,
Luke.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke, hi listfolk,

To your questions:

1. dsm.var.gam is appropriate if you think that there is no correlation
between your detectability model and your spatial model -- that is that
detection doesn't vary in space. This can be the case when you have, for
example, Beaufort in your detection function which will vary as you move
over the survey when at sea. If you don't have any covariates in your
detection function, you can't tell whether that is happening, so
dsm.var.gam is fine. dsm.var.prop will try to estimate the covariance
between the detection model and the spatial model.

2. Not necessarily. I think it's always safer to do the whole thing
again if you're going to change the response.

3. We don't have guidance on cross-validation at the moment, but this is
something I'm working on this year as part of a US Navy-funded project.
I'll report back on this when I have a better handle on what works well.
You may find these papers useful though:

https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2011.00170.x

http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/cobi.12856 (appendices)

Hope this helps!

best,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

Sorry for more questions so soon.

1. Should explanatory variables for the DSM/GAM be normally distributed (or close to normal), or rather their residuals, even if this requires transformation? I understand that the response variable in a GAM does not need to be normally distributed but I have not been able to find much information, nor a consistent answer, anywhere regarding the predictor variables.

2. Can you provide any advice on selecting predictor variables to keep in the DSM when none are showing up as significant according to p-values in the DSM/GAM but a reasonable amount of deviance is being explained by the model e.g. 40+%? I am planning on trying different segment sizes in the DSM to see if this makes a difference but I am also curious if the distribution of predictor variables will have an effect (hence my question above) and I am also considering trying Principal Components in the DSM to see if this improves predictor significance and model performance.

Any guidance you can provide is appreciated.

Many thanks,

Luke.

messages.body_plain:
The past six months has seen lots of activity on our part. 🎉 There has been lots of programming activity to enhance the capabilities of the R package `Distance`, giving it most of the capabilities of the Distance for Windows software.  In addition, a new R package `dssd` has been developed to perform distance sampling survey design in R.

A brief summary of recent developments

Software
  Extensive enhancements to analytical abilities of `Distance` package
  function to perform unit conversion 📏
  specify units of measure for effort and detection distances
   function computes correct conversion factor to provide to `convert.units` argument in `ds`
  bootstrap variance estimates 👢
  including model uncertainty see http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-variance/variance-distill.html
  several types of stratification
  not only geographic stratification, but also stratification by survey type, by species (e.g. multi-species surveys)
 multipliers (and their measures of precision) are now available
 multipliers can now be stratum-specific 🖩
 numerous data sets are now included in the package 🗃️
 these are used in the extensive suite of examples available at http://examples.distancesampling.org
R package for distance sampling survey design
package `dssd` performs the functions of the design engine available in Distance for Windows

Both packages are available on CRAN now.  The Examples website shows off many of these new features.  Have a look. 🕵️

Website
  A series of case studies demonstrating the new capabilities of `Distance` and `dssd` as well as `mrds` and `dsm`.
  Case studies have been relocated to http://examples.distancesampling.org 📚
  http://distancesampling.org has been streamlined and links have been checked with dead links pruned 🪓
  Materials from August 2019 St Andrews distance sampling workshops have been posted
  http://workshops.distancesampling.org

Workshops
  registration is now open for August 2020 St Andrews distance sampling workshops 🧑‍🎓

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke, hi listfolk,

1. There are no distributional assumptions on the explanatory variables.

2. This is tricky. I don't recommend using PCA or some other
variable-globbing scheme, as you'll lose any interpretability in the
model. Have you tried just using smooths of location (projected)? This
is a kind of catch-all in the model (since all your other environmental
variables will vary in space anyway), so might get you somewhere. You
might also want to investigate including your covariates as linear terms
in the model and see whether there is much benefit to including
smoothers at all(!). Another option would be to switch basis to a
"shrinkage" approach (bs="ts" or bs="cs" in each s() term) as these will
totally remove non-useful terms in the model and you can see what's left
(normally the linear bits are left in).

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I work for the department of environment in the Cayman Islands and we are attempting to estimate the population size and to create a distribution map of an endemic bromeliad in a restricted forest site. The site is ~ 55 acres and the plant is only found here plus a few small satellite lots around the main forest. We have chosen to use systematically placed points because of the jagged karst terrain found in the study area.

I have a few questions about the design:

The plants occur in singly and in cluster ranging from a few plants to ~15 plants. The clusters occur in tight bunches and larger plants have clonal vegetative growth. We are attempting to count the rosettes of the clusters so any large plant + its satellites. However, small single plants will still be counted. The cluster size is difficult to estimate correctly from a distance. Is it right to say that the detection function allows for this type of imperfect detection?

I used the 'distance.sample.size' R package to estimate the sample size required for this survey. The estimated sample size ranges from 76 - 216 for a targeted CV = 15% depending on the dispersion parameter used (P was set to 0.5 but doesn't affect estimates in a large way).  The plant seems ubiquitous in the study area but also forms large clusters and is more abundant near wetlands. Because of its clustering pattern, I chose a dispersion parameter of 2 which results in a sample size of 120. The visibility in the forest and low and the truncation will most likely be in the range of 15 - 25 meters. This amount of coverage means that at w = 15  we cover 39% of the study area and at w= 25 we cover 105%. Is there a recommended proportion coverage for a plant and study area like this? If I use the more conservative estimate of 74 (dispersion parameter = 1) the proportion covered seems more reasonable with 23% covered at w=15 and 65% at w = 25.

I went out and did two random points and obtained 26 detections which produced the attached detection function. With more samples I expect the detection function to fill out but I think 25m will be near the maximum observable distance. I have also attached some images of plant clusters for reference. Plus, I attached an image of the survey site and 120 survey points.

messages.body_plain:
Vaughn

Several brief thoughts.  I presume the clearings within the forest are not to be considered part of your study area as you seem to intentionally avoid placing survey effort within them; is that correct?

I appreciate it may be difficult to count individuals in a cluster from the point.  However, distance sampling permits the recording of detections from the point station, then confirmation of the group size could be made by walking up to the group for closer examination.  Marine mammal researchers do this regularly by breaking from their survey transects to steam toward a group of cetaceans to obtain a better estimate of group size.  There are many forms of uncertainty in surveys that are outside your control, in this situation, uncertainty in estimation of group size in within your means to control.

Regarding the proportion of the study area that should be surveyed; there is no rigid guidance on this matter.  Going back to the analogy of marine cetacean surveys: in the remote Southern Ocean it can be prohibitive to survey much more than 1% of the study area.  Nevertheless, defensible estimates can be produced.  At the other extreme, having point stations with detection radii that overlap (your w=25 situation) where the covered region exceeds the size of the study area; can be considered problematic because of potential double counting.  However, a simulation investigation of this by Buckland (2006) suggested the overlap issue did not induce large bias.

The question of sample size in distance sampling surveys boils down to two questions: a) are there sufficient detections to properly characterise the shape of the detection function and thereby reliably estimate the probability of detecting objects within the truncation distance and b) is there adequate spatial replication of samplers (lines or points) within the study area to accurately characterise the variability in encounter rate between samplers.

You are correct there is not a general-purpose plotting function for detection functions with covariates.  As you note from your detective work, this subject has come up previously, and the function detfct() has been implicated.

I've knocked together the beginnings of a function to perform what you requested, working only with a single factor covariate.  You could expand on it to produce more elegant plots.  Points to consider along the way:  what values of continuous covariates will you want plotted (the answer is obvious for factor covariates, but not for continuous).  How many combinations of those possible do you wish to have shown?  This issues are why such a full-fledged plotting function hasn't been produced.

Nevertheless, here is a function (it will receive no points for style), but it is reproducible given the data sets in the Distance package.

library(Distance)
conversion.factor <- convert_units("meter", NULL, "hectare")
data(Savannah_sparrow_1980)
Savannah_sparrow_1980.hn.region <- ds(data=Savannah_sparrow_1980, key="hn", truncation=55,
                                      transect="point", convert.units=conversion.factor,
                                      formula=~Region.Label)
plot.with.covariates <- function(dsobject) {
#   Purpose: plot detection function for each level of factor covariate

Hi Eric,

Thanks very much for your swift reply and for the suggested approach. As I understand it, detfct() can be used to obtain predictions for some combinations of covariate values/levels but only if these appear in the original data set. Is that correct? Hence, for example, I don't think you can predict detection probabilities at say the 25th, 50th and 75th percentile of the sea state (as in Fig. 9, Campbell, et al. (2015). Deep Sea Res II, 112: 143-157), unless by chance your original data contained detections at these values.

If that is the case, imagine that there would be some appetite for a function that allowed one predict detection probabilities from a ddf object at specific distances and covariate values/levels. Users could then easily construct their own plots. Do you know if there are any plans to add such a function to Distance or any of the other related packages? Maybe not a trivial ask!

All the best,

Ewan

messages.body_plain:
Gabriele

Response to your two questions:
When objects are detected in groups, distance sampling uses the perpendicular distance recorded to the centre of the group to estimate the density of groups in the survey.  When group size is also recorded, the density of groups is multiplied by average group size to produce an estimate of density of individuals.  The average group size is derived from the recorded sizes of groups included in your data.  There is an additional consideration that small groups are less likely to be detected at large distances; this can induce a positive bias in estimated average group size.  This is because average size of detected groups is a biased estimate of size of groups in the population.  This can be taken into account by using group size as a covariate in the detection function model.
Sample.Label refers to the number of spatial replicates in the survey design.  If you have 15 transects in your study, regardless of whether they are visited once or 10 times, you still have 15 transects.  This is should be reflected in your use of Sample.Label.  The idea is to understand the variability in encounter rate throughout the study area--assessed by the encounter rate variance between spatial replicate transects.  You do need to account for multiple visits to transects; this is reflected in the Effort (or line length) in your data.  If you have a 1km transect that is visited 5 times, the effort associated with that transect in the data is 5km.

Have a look at our online distance sampling training material for more information on such details.
Chapter 5 (https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/) for information about animals in groups and covariates in the detection function

Welcome to the list.  You have the general idea of the formula correct.  We commonly write the formula in this way:
where P_a is the probability of detecting a nest given it is within distance w of the transect.  The question is how to estimate this value P_a.  That estimate is derived from fitting a detection function to the perpendicular distances you have observed.

Your data are well organised, except the file lacks the actual length of each transect; you record the distance along the transect for each detection, but you do not include the total length of each transect.

With the addition of the total transect length for each transect, you should be able to read your file into R and load the Distance package.  Change the field name "Transect" to "Sample.Label" and the field name "Perpendicular.distance.(m)" to "distance". Within the package, there is a function ds() that fits detection functions to your data.  You then choose the most appropriate model for your data and produce estimates of nest density from the output produced by the summary  function.

All of these steps are described in an introductory example of analysing line transect data at this web address
https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-lines/lines-distill.html
Note that to convert your estimate of nest density to an estimate of orangutan density, you will need to provide additional information, namely a nest production rate and a nest decay rate.  Examples of including these multipliers is provided in another example we have online:
http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-mult/multipliers-distill.html
You can also watch lectures on fundamentals of distance sampling at this website

Greetings List,

I'm working on some aerial survey data for marine mammals with independent observers. Is there a limit to which the MR model will deal with poor observer performance?  In this situation, the primary observers are experienced professionals and the secondary observers are locals. When I look at the graphs depicting observer performance (e.g. objects detected by either observer compared to observer x, for binned distances) the primary observer performance looks great while the secondary is lacking: 444 obs by primary, 114 obs by secondary and 85 by both. When I run the analysis, the MR model assigns a similar dismal probability of detection to both observers (~0.30 each and ~0.50 combined). Is the poor secondary observer performance precluding the use of this data for MR analysis?  As a 0.30 detection probability is unlikely for the primary observer (as evidenced by other survey data), it would appear that the MR analysis will give the data a positive bias? Is there a 'rule of thumb' to assess observer performance when using MR analysis?

Thanks in advance,
Mitch Firman
